title: Adjectives and participles used as nouns

objectives.can: Read an adjective or participle with the article as a noun and supply 'man', 'woman', 'thing' or 'people' from its gender and number.

explanation.summary: Greek often leaves out the noun and lets an adjective or a participle, with the article, do its work: ὁ ἀγαθός is 'the good man', τὰ ἀγαθά is 'the good things'. The article, the gender and the number tell you what the missing noun would be.

sections.heading: An adjective standing alone
body: An adjective normally describes a noun, and agrees with it in case, number and gender. But if the noun is obvious or general, Greek may drop it and keep the adjective. The adjective then acts as a noun. Grammarians call this the substantival use ('substantive' means 'noun').
In Matthew 5:8 the phrase οἱ καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ is 'the pure in heart'. Nothing in the Greek says 'people', but the article οἱ and the masculine plural ending of καθαροί do the work.

sections.heading: Gender and number tell you what to supply
body: The ending of the adjective tells you what the missing noun would have been. Masculine singular: 'the … man' or 'the one who …'. Feminine singular: 'the … woman', 'she who …'. Neuter singular: 'the … thing' or 'what is …', often an abstract idea ('what is evil'). Masculine plural: 'the … men' or 'the … people'; a masculine plural can include women. Feminine plural: 'the … women'. Neuter plural: 'the … things'.

Luke 16:25 has two neuter plurals, τὰ ἀγαθά and τὰ κακά: 'the good things' and 'the bad things'. Romans 12:9 has two neuter singulars, τὸ πονηρόν and τῷ ἀγαθῷ: 'what is evil' and 'what is good'. Case works as always: the case of the adjective shows what the whole phrase does in its clause.

sections.heading: Participles do the same
body: A participle is a verbal adjective, and it can be used in the same way. ὁ πιστεύων in John 3:18 is 'the one who believes', and the next clause has ὁ … μὴ πιστεύων, 'the one who does not believe'. The article makes the participle a noun phrase; the masculine singular supplies 'the one'.

The forms of the participle are the subject of Stage 4. For now, learn the reading habit: when you see an article followed by something that looks like an adjective or a participle, and no noun comes after it, supply a noun from the gender and number.

sections.heading: Without the article, and when the noun is there
body: The article is the usual signal, but not the only one. In Matthew 5:45, ἐπὶ πονηροὺς καὶ ἀγαθούς has no article: 'on evil and good (people)'. In Romans 8:27, ὑπὲρ ἁγίων is 'on behalf of holy ones'. Here the masculine plural ending still tells you the missing noun.

Be careful that the noun is really missing. In Luke 6:45, ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος is 'the good man'; ἀγαθός is an ordinary adjective that describes ἄνθρωπος, and there is nothing to supply. Check what follows before you decide that an adjective is standing alone.

misunderstandings: Translating ὁ ἀγαθός as the abstract 'the good'. A masculine singular normally means 'the good man', 'the good one'. For the abstract idea Greek usually uses the neuter.
Forgetting that a masculine plural can include women. οἱ ἅγιοι, 'the holy ones' or 'holy people', is not only for men.
Treating the article as part of the participle. In ὁ πιστεύων, the article is what makes the phrase a noun; it does not belong to the verb.
Supplying 'men' automatically. The gender decides: neuter plural means 'things', not 'people'.

deeper.heading: When the form does not decide
body: Some endings are the same in the masculine and the neuter. In Matthew 6:13, ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ may be 'from the evil one' (masculine) or 'from evil' (neuter), because the genitive singular looks the same in both. Interpreters disagree about which is meant, and the form alone does not settle it. When this happens, the question belongs to the context and to interpretation, and not to grammar.

examples.analysis: οἱ καθαροί is nominative plural masculine: the article plus an adjective with no noun, so supply 'people': 'the pure'. τῇ καρδίᾳ says in what respect they are pure. The phrase is the subject of the sentence about those who are blessed.

examples.analysis: τὸ πονηρόν and τῷ ἀγαθῷ are neuter singular adjectives with the article. They stand for ideas, not persons: 'what is evil' and 'what is good'. τὸ is accusative, the object of the participle ἀποστυγοῦντες; τῷ is dative, after κολλώμενοι.

examples.analysis: τὰ ἀγαθά and τὰ κακά are accusative neuter plural, with the article: 'the good things' and 'the bad things'. The first is the object of ἀπέλαβες; the second is the object of a verb that the Greek leaves unwritten, with Λάζαρος as its subject.

examples.analysis: ἡ πιστεύσασα is a feminine singular participle with the article: 'she who believed'. The feminine ending shows that a woman is meant, and the article makes the participle a noun phrase. μακαρία is the predicate adjective: 'blessed is she'.

practice.prompt: οἱ πτωχοί (words 1–2) has no noun. Whom does it describe?

options: Nobody: the phrase is incomplete without a noun
Poor people: masculine plural, so supply 'people'
Poor things: the plural is neuter
practice.explain: The article οἱ and the masculine plural ending of πτωχοί make the phrase a noun phrase meaning 'the poor'. A feminine or neuter ending would change what is supplied.

practice.prompt: What does τὰ ἀγαθά (words 7–8) stand for in this verse?

practice.explain: τὰ is nominative or accusative neuter plural, and ἀγαθά agrees. The neuter plural supplies 'things'. Here it is accusative, the object of ἀπέλαβες.

practice.prompt: ὁ ἐραυνῶν (words 0–2) is an article with a participle and no noun. How do you read it?

options: The one who searches: masculine singular
practice.explain: The article ὁ is masculine singular, and so is the participle. 'The one who searches' is the natural reading; τὰς καρδίας is its object.

practice.prompt: οἱ πενθοῦντες (words 1–2) is a participle with the article. How do you read it?

options: No: an adjective without an article cannot be a noun
Yes, but only because the verb is singular
Yes: it is masculine plural, 'blind people', the subject of ἀναβλέπουσιν
Yes: it is neuter singular, 'a blind thing'
practice.explain: The article is the usual signal, but not the only one. τυφλοί is nominative plural masculine, and with no noun to describe it stands for 'blind people'. The verb ἀναβλέπουσιν is plural to match.

check.prompt: ὁ πιστεύων (words 0–1) has an article and a participle and no noun. How do you read it?

options: The one who believes: masculine singular
check.explain: Both the article and the participle are masculine singular, so supply 'one' or 'man': 'the one who believes'. A plural would need οἱ πιστεύοντες.

check.prompt: ἡ πιστεύσασα (words 2–3) is a participle with the article. Who is meant?

check.explain: ἡ is feminine singular, and so is πιστεύσασα. The feminine ending shows that the one meant is a woman. The masculine would be ὁ πιστεύσας.

check.prompt: τὸ γεγεννημένον (words 0–1) is neuter singular. What does it refer to?

options: A thing or what is born: 'that which is born'
check.explain: The article τό and the participle are neuter singular, so supply 'that which' or 'what'. It does not name a person. The prepositional phrase that follows says from what it was born.

check.prompt: Compare τοὺς σοφούς (words 10–11) with τὰ μωρά (words 1–2). How do their genders change what is supplied?

options: τοὺς σοφούς is masculine plural, 'wise people'; τὰ μωρά is neuter plural, 'foolish things'
Both mean 'people', because both are plural
τοὺς σοφούς is neuter, 'wise things'; τὰ μωρά is masculine, 'foolish people'
Neither can stand alone without a noun
check.explain: Number is the same, plural, but gender differs. The masculine supplies persons, the neuter supplies things. τοὺς is accusative masculine plural and τὰ is accusative neuter plural.

check.prompt: οἱ νεκροί (words 11–12): what does the phrase mean?

check.explain: Masculine plural with the article: 'the dead'. It is the subject of ἀκούσουσιν. Death as an idea would be a neuter singular.

check.prompt: Is ἀγαθός (word 1) used alone as a noun here?

options: No: it is an ordinary adjective describing ἄνθρωπος; no noun needs to be supplied
Yes: it means 'the good one' and ἄνθρωπος is a second subject
Yes, because it has the article
check.explain: ἄνθρωπος is present and agrees with ἀγαθός in case, number and gender: 'the good man'. Only when the noun is missing do we supply one. The article does not by itself make an adjective a noun.

check.prompt: τὸ πονηρόν (words 4–5) is neuter singular. What does it name?

options: What is evil: an idea rather than a person
check.explain: The neuter singular is the usual way to speak of an idea or a quality: 'what is evil', 'evil'. A person would need the masculine or feminine.

check.prompt: The adjectives πονηροὺς and ἀγαθούς (words 15 and 17) have no article and no noun. What do they stand for?

options: A single evil and good person
Evil and good people: masculine plural
An evil and a good woman
check.explain: Both are accusative masculine plural after ἐπί, so supply 'people': 'on evil and good (people)'. There is no article, and the phrase is a general one.

check.prompt: ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ is genitive singular. What does the form alone tell you about the noun to supply?

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: It can be masculine ('the evil one') or neuter ('evil'): the ending is the same
check.explain: The genitive singular masculine and neuter look alike in this declension, so the ending leaves both open. Which is meant is decided by context and interpretation. The tempting wrong answer is to treat the form as if it settled the matter.

reading.why: The Beatitudes: eight verses, nearly every one built on an article with an adjective or a participle and no noun.
